title: The builder never judges its own work
when: Reviewing a storyboard, a drawing, an edit or a render.
summary: Whoever built a piece sees what they meant, not what is there. A fresh reviewer, ideally a different model, gets only the work itself, the brief and the owner's words, never the builder's reasoning or list of fixes, and finds the problems itself.
do: Have the other connected AI review what one AI built.
Give the reviewer the artifact, the brief and the owner's words only.
Ask for problems with their moment and evidence.
avoid: Reviews that read the builder's notes about what it fixed.
source: motion-video-kit (echris6, MIT), pinned e4b1c00: the Gauntlet loop; restated.

title: Fix the biggest gap first, then verify item by item
when: Acting on a review of a storyboard, edit or render.
summary: Do not average away a weak opening with strengths elsewhere. Fix the largest meaningful problem first. The next review checks every earlier item as fixed, partly fixed or still present, and looks for new problems the fixes caused.
steps: Rank findings by how much they hurt the video.
Re-check each earlier finding: fixed, partly, still present.
Look for regressions the fixes caused.
Stop at the quality bar or when what is left is cosmetic.
source: motion-video-kit (MIT), pinned e4b1c00: Gauntlet rules 5-7; restated.

title: One persistent actor carries the viewer through a section
when: Planning a section of several shots about one idea.
summary: Unrelated reveals in sequence feel like a slideshow, however well each is animated. Let one thing keep its identity across the shots of a section (a character, a coin, a card, a line, a shape) so the viewer follows it from shot to shot.
do: Name the persistent actor of each section in the scene direction.
Hand it from shot to shot at the same place on screen where possible.
avoid: A new unrelated subject in every shot of the same idea.
checks: Each section has something that carries across its shots.
source: motion-video-kit (MIT), pinned e4b1c00: motion grammar rule 2; restated.

title: Let the foreground become the transition
when: Moving from one scene to the next.
summary: The strongest transitions have no empty gap: a word, shape or object scales through the camera or wipes across while the next scene is already in place underneath, or a selected thing expands into the next scene.
do: Use an object or word of the outgoing shot to reveal the next one.
Pre-place the destination so the carried thing lands on it.
avoid: Fading to an empty background between scenes.
source: motion-video-kit (MIT), pinned e4b1c00: motion grammar rule 1 and mechanism catalog; restated.

title: Every animated action visibly produces a result
when: Any shot where something is done: a trade, a press, a choice, a calculation.
summary: Show the purpose as cause and effect: the trade gives the pebbles, the press changes the state, the choice opens the next door. Motion that produces nothing reads as decoration.
do: After an action, show its result in the same or next shot.
avoid: Actions whose outcome the viewer never sees.
source: motion-video-kit (MIT), pinned e4b1c00: motion grammar rule 6; restated.

title: Readable target, fast exit, slowing arrival
when: Timing camera moves, entrances and exits.
summary: Do not drift at one constant speed. Hold what must be read, leave it quickly, and ease into the next landing so the eye can read again.
do: Hold reading targets, exit fast, ease into arrivals.
source: motion-video-kit (MIT), pinned e4b1c00: motion grammar rule 4; restated.

title: The lead subject fills most of the frame; frame zero is finished
when: Composing feature beats, the hook and the ending.
summary: Empty space reads as cheap. In feature beats the lead subject fills about 60-85% of the usable frame; there are no dead colour bands; the first frame of the video is a finished composition, not a half-entered word; the final card stays readable for about 1.5-2 seconds.
do: Make the subject large in feature beats.
Start the video on a complete composition.
Hold the ending long enough to read.
avoid: A small figure in a large empty field when the shot is about that figure.
checks: The first frame of the video shows a complete picture.
source: motion-video-kit (MIT), pinned e4b1c00: quality bar; restated.

title: Vary composition types across a section
when: Planning several shots in a row.
summary: Repeating one composition (a heading above three items, a figure in the centre) makes a video feel templated. Rotate through wide establishing views, close details, overhead plans, typographic impact frames and two-shots, keeping one or two reading targets at a time.
do: Change the composition type from shot to shot within a section.
Keep at most two reading targets per frame.
avoid: The same layout three shots running.
checks: No three consecutive shots share one composition.
source: motion-video-kit (MIT), pinned e4b1c00: composition rules; restated.

title: Frozen time stays under a second per half minute
when: Checking an edit or render for dead moments.
summary: Stretches where frames barely change are measured, not guessed. Keep the total under about one second per 30 seconds and no single hold over about 0.6 seconds, except the final card.
checks: Total frozen time is under about 1 s per 30 s.
No single still stretch is longer than about 0.6 s outside the ending.
source: motion-video-kit (MIT), pinned e4b1c00: quality bar measured checks; restated.

title: Words never collide, even mid-transition
when: Words move, change or cross a transition.
summary: Titles spliced by a wipe, words flying through other words and one title over another mid-crossfade are the most noticed defects. The outgoing title leaves before the wipe; the incoming one enters after it; words that move fade out and back in at their new place.
do: Clear outgoing words before a wipe or crossfade.
Bring incoming words in after the transition.
avoid: Two words overlapping at any frame.
source: motion-video-kit (MIT), pinned e4b1c00: what critics caught in practice; restated.

title: A catalog of reusable moves for designed shots
when: Choosing how a designed shot shows an idea.
summary: Proven moves to choose from rather than inventing a new trick each time: selection that expands into the next view; a shell that appears and then fills its regions in order; lines that survive a change and connect two states; one continuous canvas the camera travels over; a stack of cards that fans out or collapses into one; a wall of information collapsing to one clear subject; an object separating into its layers and recombining; a carousel with one bright item.
do: Pick the move that matches the idea's logic.
Use each move once or twice per video.
source: motion-video-kit (MIT), pinned e4b1c00: mechanism catalog distilled from 28 films; restated.
